name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,215

clue.text: Eastern picture — a large-scale film?

blocks.note: E is the standard abbreviation for east or eastern
pic is informal shorthand for a picture or photograph

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether an oriental painting might count as a grand cinematic production.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash makes the clue read as one thought, but it simply separates the wordplay from the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An epic is a long, lavish movie with a sweeping story, huge cast and grand spectacle.

clue.text: Sort of coloured garment restricted you once

definitions.note: the answer is the colouring method; the clue names a garment made that way

blocks.note: tied means bound or restricted
ye is the old form of you

explanation.surface: A fancy patterned outfit once felt too tight on the wearer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Once' signals an archaic word, so 'you once' is the old pronoun YE.
explanation.definitionFit: Tie-dye describes cloth knotted before dyeing to make swirling patterns, a style familiar from hippie T-shirts.

clue.text: Woman and boy ending in Torquay

indicators.note: an ending is the final part, so only the closing letter of the following word is wanted

blocks.note: a lad is a boy
final letter of the place name

explanation.surface: A woman and a young lad finish their trip in an English seaside resort.
explanation.walkthrough: Torquay is a seaside town in Devon, England; only its final letter is used. 'Woman' is the definition, with 'and' joining the boy to that letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Lady is a polite or formal word for any woman, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: Fantastic cash in no time, with introduction of a movement abandoning manual processes

indicators.note: something fantastic is wild and fanciful, so the letters are freely rearranged

blocks.note: taken letter for letter as written
the article added to the other letters

explanation.surface: Making a fortune instantly by bringing in a trend that ends hand labour sounds too good to be true.
explanation.walkthrough: The extra A joins the twelve letters of 'cash in no time' before the whole lot is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Mechanisation is the shift from hand labour to machines, a trend that leaves manual work behind.

clue.text: Greek character on river eating one nourishing substance

indicators.note: in a down entry, one thing on another sits above it, so this piece comes first
to eat something is to take it inside, so one piece swallows the other

blocks.note: nu is the thirteenth letter of the Greek alphabet
the Trent is a major river in the English Midlands
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A Greek person by a riverbank is snacking on something wholesome.
explanation.walkthrough: The Trent is an English river, a favourite of setters; I goes inside it, and NU sits on top.
explanation.definitionFit: A nutrient is any compound in food that the body uses for growth and energy.

clue.text: Domain that has no edges

blocks.note: first meaning: an area of activity or influence
second meaning: a perfectly round solid with no corners or edges

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads like a description of a boundless territory; really it gives two separate senses of one word, the second geometric.
explanation.definitionFit: A field of influence is called a sphere, and the round geometric solid has a smooth surface without any edges.

clue.text: Salvation Army limited by less sophisticated evangelist

indicators.note: something limited by another is hemmed in on both sides, so it sits within

blocks.note: SA is the usual abbreviation for the Salvation Army
cruder means rougher, less refined

explanation.surface: The Salvation Army is held back by a preacher with rough manners.
explanation.walkthrough: The Salvation Army is a Christian charity, so the surface stays religious throughout; its initials go inside the comparative.
explanation.definitionFit: A crusader campaigns zealously for a cause, as an evangelist promotes a belief with missionary zeal.

clue.text: Proper tea arranged for archbishop

indicators.note: arranged means put into a new order, so these letters are reordered

blocks.note: prim means proper and formal
taken as written before rearranging

explanation.surface: A proper cup of tea has been laid on for a visiting senior churchman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Proper tea' sounds like a set phrase, but 'Proper' is a separate synonym and only 'tea' is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: In Anglican and Catholic churches, the senior archbishop of a country holds the title of primate.

clue.text: Superior meal in the evening without a starter

indicators.note: a starter is the opening course, so going without one drops the opening letter

blocks.note: supper is an evening meal

explanation.surface: A fine evening dinner served with no first course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starter' plays on the meal theme: a first course, but here the first letter of the word for the meal.
explanation.definitionFit: Upper and superior both describe something higher in position, rank or quality.

clue.text: Golf attendant, bad guy, starts to diddle you

indicators.note: the starts of words are their opening letters, so each of the next words gives its first

blocks.note: a cad is a man who behaves dishonourably
opening letters of both words

explanation.surface: A villainous bag-carrier on the golf course sets out to cheat you.
explanation.walkthrough: To diddle is British slang for swindle, which suits the surface; here only its first letter is used, plus that of 'you'.
explanation.definitionFit: A caddy carries a golfer's clubs and offers advice during the round, so is a course attendant.

clue.text: House mother finally catches insects

indicators.note: finally points to the very end, so only the closing letter of the word is kept

blocks.note: HO is the abbreviation for house
final letter of the word
nets as a verb means catches, as with fish

explanation.surface: At home, the mother at last manages to trap some stinging bugs.
explanation.walkthrough: HO for house is seen in addresses and abbreviations; 'catches' is a verb meaning traps, not a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Hornets are large stinging wasps, a particular kind of insect.

clue.text: Quiet relaxation before performing in city

indicators.note: before means coming ahead of something else, so these parts follow in sequence

blocks.note: p (piano) is the musical marking for quiet
rest is relaxation
a performer is on, onstage

explanation.surface: An entertainer takes a calm break before going onstage in town.
explanation.walkthrough: Preston is a city in Lancashire, north-west England. P for quiet comes from musical notation.
explanation.definitionFit: Preston was granted city status in 2002, so it is a straightforward example of a city.

clue.text: Dad’s dark colour or fair?

blocks.note: pa is dad, and the possessive adds S
sable is black, a heraldic and poetic word for dark

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether father's hair is dark or light.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fair' looks like the opposite of a dark colour, meaning blond, but it means moderately good.
explanation.definitionFit: Fair in the sense of middling, adequate or acceptable is the same as passable.

clue.text: Toilet surmounted by brown lines

indicators.note: in a down entry, being surmounted means having something placed on top, so that part comes first

blocks.note: tan is a light brown
the gents is a British term for a men's toilet

explanation.surface: A lavatory has brown stripes painted along the top.
explanation.walkthrough: The gents is the British name for a men's public toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: A tangent is a geometric straight line that touches a curve at one point, so tangents are lines.

clue.text: Correct this writer in margin

indicators.note: in means placed inside, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: 'this writer' is the setter referring to themself
a margin is an edge or end

explanation.surface: An author scribbles a correction in the page margin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This writer' is the setter's way of saying ME. The surface pictures marginal notes, but the margin is just an edge.
explanation.definitionFit: To emend is to correct a text, removing errors, so the verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Something that could get one carried away

definitions.text: Something that could get one carried away

blocks.clueFragment: Something that could get one carried away
blocks.note: surface reading: something thrilling enough to overwhelm a person's emotions
setter's reading: a covered chair in which a passenger is physically carried by bearers

explanation.walkthrough: 'Carried away' suggests excitement, but taken literally it describes being borne along by porters, as in the old enclosed chair carried on poles.
explanation.definitionFit: A sedan chair was an enclosed seat on poles in which one person was transported by two bearers.

clue.text: Party attire that is folded over

blocks.note: a do is a party or social event
gear is clothing

explanation.surface: Party clothes that have been creased or folded double.
explanation.walkthrough: A do is a British informal word for a party.
explanation.definitionFit: A dog-ear is the corner of a page turned down like a floppy ear, a bent flap of paper.

clue.text: Learner enthralled by puzzle-maker — one ensconced in new territory?

indicators.note: to be enthralled is to be held captive, so one piece is held inside another

blocks.note: L is for learner, as on British learner-driver plates
a setter compiles crosswords

explanation.surface: A beginner is captivated by a crossword compiler, someone who has found a new home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Enthralled' means charmed in the surface, but literally means held captive, which is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A settler is a person who makes a home in a newly colonised or unfamiliar land.

clue.text: Made a note of unusual old egg

indicators.note: unusual means out of the ordinary, so the letters fall out of their ordinary order

blocks.note: taken as written before rearranging

explanation.surface: Someone jotted down a record of a strange, ancient egg.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unusual old egg' reads as a description of a curiosity; the last two words are the letters to reorder.
explanation.definitionFit: To log something is to record it formally, as in a ship's log or diary entry.

clue.text: Add to workers in month, having let us go

indicators.note: letting go means releasing, so those named letters are dropped
in means placed inside, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: men is a common word for workers
a month of the year, which loses two letters

explanation.surface: A firm takes on extra staff for a month after dismissing the speaker and colleagues.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Us' is taken literally as the letters U and S, removed from the month; the workers then go into what remains.
explanation.definitionFit: To augment something is to increase or supplement it, making it larger.

clue.text: Outfit needed by the Spanish star

blocks.note: a rig is an outfit of clothes
el is the Spanish masculine word for the

explanation.surface: A Spanish celebrity requires a costume.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Star' tempts as a celebrity, given the outfit; it is a real star in the night sky.
explanation.definitionFit: Rigel is a bright blue supergiant in the constellation Orion, one of the most visible stars.

clue.text: Impolite daughter getting in Parisian’s way

indicators.note: getting in means entering, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: D is the abbreviation for daughter
rue is French for street

explanation.surface: A bad-mannered girl obstructs a man from Paris.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting in someone's way' sounds like obstruction; here the way is a French street.
explanation.definitionFit: Rude and impolite both describe behaviour that lacks good manners.

clue.text: Girl in glasses

indicators.note: in means contained within, so the letters sit inside the following word

blocks.note: letters two to five of the word

explanation.surface: A young woman wearing spectacles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In glasses' reads as wearing spectacles, but the girl is literally inside the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Lass is a Scottish and northern English word for a girl or young woman.

clue.text: Smallest line with particular direction

blocks.note: L is the abbreviation for line
east is one compass direction

explanation.surface: The shortest line drawn heading one way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Particular direction' is vague on purpose: any compass point could fit, and only EAST makes a word.
explanation.definitionFit: Least is the superlative of little, meaning the tiniest amount or degree.

clue.text: Strange quality that fifteen will show

blocks.note: first meaning: peculiarity or weirdness
second meaning: the property of a number not divisible by two

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fifteen' looks like a cross-reference to another clue, but it is simply the number, which is not divisible by two.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun covers both peculiarity of character and the arithmetical property of whole numbers like fifteen that leave remainder one.
